title: IT in the business environment
blurb: Why information is needed, its qualities, IT delivery, outsourcing and processing.

topics.name: Why businesses need information
topics.line: Nine reasons managers need information, from planning to decision making.
topics.remember: Planning, Controlling, Recording transactions, Performance measurement, Communication, SCM, Sales and marketing, Employee management, Decision making
topics.simple: A business is run with decisions. Managers need information to plan, to check progress, to keep records, to talk to people and to decide.
frames: Planning: work out how to carry out the strategy.
Controlling: check if the work is on track.
Performance measurement: compare what happened with the plan.
Decision making: choose using the information.
gls: supply chain management, optimising businesses that work together to deliver a product
checking implementation and correcting any deviation
comparing actual outcome with the plan

topics.name: Types of information
topics.line: Strategic, tactical, operational and planning information.
topics.remember: Strategic: board, long-term, estimates. Tactical: middle managers, short-term. Operational: front line, day-to-day. Planning: implementation steps.
topics.simple: Information is sorted by how it is used. The board looks far ahead. Middle managers watch the month. Front-line staff do the daily work.
frames: Strategic: the board asks if resources can be made available to expand production.
Tactical: middle managers read monthly variance reports for the factory.
Operational: front-line staff need to know how many operatives one shift needs.
Planning: a team prepares a budget for the next financial year.
gls: long-term, often based on estimates, broad picture
day-to-day, routine, very detailed, mostly accurate

topics.name: Qualities of good information
topics.remember: ACCURATE: Accurate, Complete, Cost-beneficial, User-targeted, Relevant, Authoritative, Timely, Easy to use. Accountability is not one of them.
topics.simple: Good information is not just a lot of numbers. It must be correct, complete, worth its cost, suited to the reader, useful, trusted, on time and easy to use.
frames: Accurate: the figures add up and have no typing errors.
User-targeted: a CEO sees a dashboard of KPIs, not a 5,000-line listing.
Timely: a daily overdraft report arrives each morning, so managers act the same day.
Easy to use: a colour-coded dashboard beats a 50-page printout.
gls: the source is reliable and credible
does not cost more to get than the benefit it gives
only what the decision needs, however interesting the rest looks

cards.mean: Figures add up, rounding is appropriate, no typing errors, correct categories, assumptions stated
cards.ex: A variance report that ties back to the general ledger.

cards.mean: Includes everything it needs, relevant external data and prior-year comparatives
cards.ex: A report with current-year and prior-year figures.

cards.mean: Should not cost more to obtain than the benefit it gives
cards.ex: A detailed cost analysis only when the decision justifies it.

cards.mean: Tailored to the user: summaries for senior managers, detail for junior managers
cards.ex: A CEO dashboard of KPIs, not a 5,000-line listing.

cards.mean: Leave out what the decision does not need, however interesting
cards.ex: A sales report with regional totals, not every invoice.

cards.mean: The source must be reliable and credible, including internet sources
cards.ex: A recognised industry body, not an anonymous website.

cards.mean: Available when needed. Annual reports are too infrequent for day-to-day control
cards.ex: A daily overdraft report each morning.

cards.mean: Clearly presented, not too long, sent by the right channel
cards.ex: A colour-coded dashboard rather than a 50-page printout.

topics.name: What makes information valuable?
topics.line: Four factors decide how valuable information is.
topics.remember: Source, Ease of assimilation, Accessibility, Relevance. Value is not based on scarcity.
topics.simple: Information is valuable when you can trust where it came from, understand it quickly, reach it easily and use it for your own decision.
frames: Source: a respected source such as Reuters can be relied on.
Ease of assimilation: dashboards and graphics make it easier to understand.
Accessibility: if it is on the internet, users save time and effort.
Relevance: news about a new plastic matters to a car maker, not a software house.
gls: taking information in and understanding it
how easily users can reach it

cards.mean: A respected, well-known source such as Reuters is relied on with more confidence
cards.ex: News from Reuters is trusted more than an unknown page.

cards.mean: Colour, graphics, infographics, dashboards, sound and movement make information easier to understand
cards.ex: A dashboard is quicker to read than a table of numbers.

cards.mean: If it is in an easily accessible place, such as the internet, users save time and effort
cards.ex: Looking it up online instead of searching files.

cards.mean: Value is not based on scarcity. It depends on whether it is useful to the specific user
cards.ex: Plastic news: valuable to a car maker, irrelevant to a software house.

items.q: A respected, well-known source such as Reuters
items.why: A respected source gives more confidence.

items.q: Dashboards and graphics make information easier to understand

items.why: Value depends on usefulness to the user, which is relevance.

items.q: Information is valuable because it is scarce
items.why: Wrong: value is not based on scarcity, it depends on relevance to the user.

topics.name: Cost and value of information
topics.line: Is it worth getting more information?
topics.remember: Unused information has no actual value. Extra benefit must beat extra cost. An MIS enquiry costs effectively zero.
topics.simple: Information only has value when someone acts on it. Before collecting more, compare the extra benefit with the extra cost.
frames: A manager could collect more information.
It would improve profit by NPR 9,000.
But it costs NPR 10,000 to collect, so the net value is negative.
An MIS enquiry costs almost nothing, because the system is already paid for.
gls: already paid, so it does not rise with each enquiry

cards.mean: Information that is obtained but not used has no actual value
cards.ex: A report that nobody reads.

cards.mean: What the extra information is expected to gain
cards.ex: A profit improvement of NPR 9,000.

cards.mean: What it costs to obtain the extra information
cards.ex: NPR 10,000 to collect it.

cards.mean: Effectively zero: the MIS and the enquiry software are already bought
cards.ex: Fixed costs are already incurred, so each enquiry adds no meaningful cost.

items.q: Extra benefit NPR 9,000, extra cost NPR 10,000
items.why: The net value is negative, so it is not worth having.

items.q: Extra benefit NPR 15,000, extra cost NPR 10,000
items.why: The extra benefit is greater than the extra cost.

items.q: Information that is obtained but never used
items.why: Value only arises from actions taken, so unused information has no value.

topics.name: IT delivery and IT support
topics.line: Two sets of IT activities and four management actions.
topics.remember: Delivery: operations, capacity, billing, service levels, continuity. Support: infrastructure, integrity, security, incidents.
topics.simple: IT delivery keeps the services running for users. IT support looks after the infrastructure behind them. Two teams can do the two jobs.
frames: Delivery: data extraction, report production and report distribution.
Delivery: capacity is monitored and service continuity is planned.
Support: hardware, software and networks are kept configured.
Support: security, access control and fixing incidents.
gls: a problem to prevent, investigate and resolve

cards.mean: Data extraction, report production and report distribution
cards.ex: Producing and sending the daily report.

cards.mean: Keep watching how much capacity is used
cards.ex: Seeing the server is nearly full.

cards.mean: A delivery activity
cards.ex: Billing users for IT services.

cards.mean: Business operations stay available to the agreed standard
cards.ex: The system is up when the business needs it.

cards.mean: Keep service going if something fails
cards.ex: A plan for when the server stops.

cards.mean: Maintaining hardware, software and networks
cards.ex: Keeping computers and the network set up correctly.

cards.mean: Keeping the infrastructure intact
cards.ex: Protecting equipment and the data on it.

cards.mean: Control who can use what
cards.ex: Passwords and permissions.

cards.mean: Prevention, investigation and resolution
cards.ex: Finding why a system failed and fixing it.

cards.mean: Stay aware of rapid IT developments such as cloud computing, automation and intelligent systems
cards.ex: Not missing a useful new tool.

cards.mean: Careful planning so IT changes run smoothly and without disruption
cards.ex: Scheduling an upgrade for a quiet time.

cards.mean: Prioritise and document IT tasks, with a rolling programme of business-as-usual and forward-change work
cards.ex: A written list of tasks in priority order.

cards.mean: Recruit and retain staff with suitable data science skills in suitable roles
cards.ex: Hiring an analyst for a data role.

topics.name: Outsourcing
topics.line: Contracting a function out to an external provider.
topics.remember: Outsourcing: contracting out a specific business function to an external provider. Benefits: focus, better service. Challenges: formality, arm's length, SLAs.
topics.simple: Outsourcing means paying another company to do one job for you, such as running your IT. You gain focus, but you control it from a distance.
frames: The business hands one function to an outside provider.
A service level agreement (SLA) sets what the provider must deliver.
The business can focus on its core activities.
But the service is managed at arm's length, so direct control is reduced.
gls: contracting out a specific business function to an external provider
service level agreement, negotiated in the contract
managed from a distance, not directly

cards.mean: The business concentrates on what it does best
cards.ex: A shop leaves IT running to a specialist.

cards.mean: Access to better IT functions and service than in-house staff can give
cards.ex: A specialist team with more skills.

cards.mean: The IT function has to be managed more formally
cards.ex: A contract and regular reviews.

cards.mean: The service is managed at a distance, so there is less direct control
cards.ex: You cannot walk over and direct the team.

cards.mean: Service level agreements must be carefully negotiated
cards.ex: Agreeing response times in the SLA.

items.q: The business can focus on its core activities
Service is managed at arm's length
items.why: Reduced direct control is a challenge.

items.q: Access to better IT service than in-house staff

topics.name: Information processing: CATIVA
topics.line: Six criteria that processing must meet.
topics.remember: CATIVA: Completeness, Accuracy, Timeliness, Inalterability, Verifiability, Assessability. Non-repudiation is not on the list.
topics.simple: Processing turns data into information. To trust the result, the processing must be complete, accurate, on time, tamper-proof, traceable and open to checking.
frames: Completeness: everything that needs processing is processed.
Accuracy: the output stays true to its sources and has no errors.
Inalterability: unauthorised people cannot change the process.
Verifiability: the audit trail can be followed from source to information.
gls: the process cannot be altered while running or once completed
the data trail, also called the audit trail, can be followed
the effectiveness of processing is open to scrutiny

cards.mean: Everything that needs to be processed is processed. Nothing is omitted
cards.ex: No invoice is left out of the total.

cards.mean: Processing keeps data true to its sources and the information has no errors
cards.ex: The report figures match the source.

cards.mean: Processing happens in line with data availability and information needs, often in real time
cards.ex: Sales appear in the report as they happen.

cards.mean: The process cannot be altered by unauthorised persons while running or once completed
cards.ex: Only authorised people can change the system.

cards.mean: The data trail from source through processing to information can be followed (the audit trail)
cards.ex: Tracing a report figure back to the invoice.

cards.mean: The effectiveness of processing is open to scrutiny so its quality can be judged
cards.ex: A review shows the processing works well.

regions.label: Six criteria the processing must meet
